items.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: But I had to like give them music of James Brown and I’m trying to think who else, as much of music that sounded like what we were trying to do so that they can get a context.

ctx.x: I can imagine David [Murray] in that scenario too. He’s got such big ears that I’m sure that that was just really great for him to deal with something new.

David is, yeah, he’s just, I can’t say that — he’s just on an amazing high level. And just my brief experience of us working together just elevated me on a level. And he’s just very generous and patient. And last year I was commissioned by the Rockefeller Multi- Arts Production Fund, the San Francisco Arts Commission and Meet the Composer in New York to compose a work called “Up From the Root” which was to celebrate Chinese-American identity, Chinese diaspora specifically. Because I’d attended a conference where…

called “Sweet Whisper of a Flower” that I composed. And it has — I hate to use the word influences — but it’s from my study of music of Wayne Shorter and Billy Strayhorn in terms of how they use color and timbre. And so what I did was I took a Chinese melody like the “Golden Snake Dance,” and put in a different tempo that was more like a ballad impressionistic. And then I wrote a countermelody that had characteristics of a Chinese folk melody but placed in different beats, places, accents, so that it would be…
